newsitem.title: ITALY: Fate of Italy govt linked to welfare - hard-left.
newsitem.headline: Fate of Italy govt linked to welfare - hard-left.

text.p: The fate of Prime Minister Romano Prodi's government depends on how it handles the sensitive issue of welfare reform, Fausto Bertinotti, leader of the hard-left Communist Refoundation party, said on Monday.

The centre-left coalition is due to start talks with union leaders on Tuesday over possible changes to social spending and many economists are urging a fresh overhaul of pensions, just two years after the last reform of the generous state system.
Refoundation, which guarantees Prodi's majority in the lower house of parliament, has said it will not support any cuts in welfare expenditure and sees little need for pension changes.

"The future of the Prodi government depends on the welfare state. We hope that the ruling majority consolidates itself around the question of social reform," Bertinotti said in a television interview.
"The majority must have, if not a joint position, then at least a common viewpoint to put to the other forces," he said.
Centrist parties within the Prodi coalition have called on the government to usher in structural welfare savings to keep the large state deficit under control.

With time running out for Italy to win a place in the starting line-up for the single European currency, the government is expected to indicate hoped-for savings when it publishes its three-year economic programme for the period 1998-2000, later this month.

The European Commission recommended to EU member states on Monday that they tell Italy it had to do much more to bring its 1998 deficit below three percent of GDP as demanded by the Maastricht Treaty.
The deficit/GDP ratio in 1996 was 6.7 percent.
The Commission also said Italy should replace one-off measures it had taken in 1997 to reach economic and monetary targets (EMU) with "structural measures with a permanent impact on the budget".

The independent Italian economic research centre (CER) said in a survey published on Monday in Rome that Italy should seek savings of more than six trillion lire ($3.57 billion) on social spending and public services in 1998.

These savings should rise to eight trillion lire in 1999 and 10 trillion lire in the year 2000. It added that a 1995 pension reform should be speeded up and immediate savings sought from the health budget.
"It would not make sense to use resourses freed from some areas to be used to increase spending in other sectors," the report said.
However Bertinotti on Monday restated his belief that there should be no reduction in welfare spending. "The welfare state has to be reformed, not cut," he said.
